meta.descriptionEn: On November 18, 1929, a magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck the seabed south of Newfoundland. Minutes later, transatlantic cables began snapping one after another, farther and farther down the slope. Then the sea itself struck the Burin Peninsula, with waves that destroyed communities and cut off all communication, and a blizzard struck the day after. For years nobody understood what had broken twelve cables in 28 places. The answer, pieced together by scientists in 1952, revealed an underwater avalanche and the first documented turbidity current. Follow the timeline of the tremor, the waves, the rescue, and the puzzle that still shapes how we protect the cables carrying the world's data today.
meta.descriptionUr: 18 November 1929 ko Newfoundland ke jenub mein samandar ke neeche 7.2 shiddat ka zalzala aaya. Chand minutes baad atlantic ki telegraph cables aik ke baad aik toot-ti chali gayin. Phir tsunami ne Burin Peninsula ke gaon tabah kar diye aur har rabta kat gaya. Scientists ko barson baad samajh aaya ke samandar ke andar pani mein ghuli resh (sediment) ka tezi se behta hua rela, yaani turbidity current, chal raha tha. Is documentary mein dekhein ke yeh sab kaise hua, logon ne kya jhela, aur aaj bhi yeh kahani internet cables ki hifazat ke liye kyun ahem hai.

articleEn: On 18 November 1929, a powerful earthquake struck beneath the Atlantic Ocean, roughly 400 kilometres south of Newfoundland. Its moment magnitude was 7.2, and the shaking was felt as far away as New York City and Montreal. But the real story was unfolding not on land but deep under the sea.

Transatlantic telegraph cables on the seabed began to break, one after another. The breaks spread away from the epicenter and down the slope, until 12 cables in all had snapped. Then a tsunami rose and reached the coast in three waves, crashing into the small coastal towns of Newfoundland.

This raises several questions. What happened on the seafloor to cut so many cables? Was the shock of the earthquake alone to blame? How did the waves hit the shore, how high were they, and what happened to the people there? And most importantly, what did scientists discover years later?

Today we tell the full story of the 1929 Grand Banks earthquake, also known as the Laurentian Slope earthquake and the South Shore Disaster. It is not just the story of one earthquake. It is also the story of a discovery that revealed a silent force hidden beneath the sea.

articleEn: To understand this story, we have to go back several decades before 1929. The idea of laying wires under the sea became reality in the 1850s. These submarine communications cables were laid on the ocean floor so that telegraph messages could travel from one shore to another. For the first time, they created instant communication between continents. By 1872, every continent except Antarctica was connected by submarine cables.

A great dream was to lay a cable across the Atlantic. The first transatlantic telegraph cable began working on 16 August 1858, but the dream proved unfinished. Cyrus West Field persuaded British industrialists to provide funding, yet the technology of the time could not handle the project, and the cable worked for only about a month. New attempts followed in 1865 and 1866 with SS Great Eastern, the largest steamship in the world, and these produced the first successful transatlantic cable.

Early cables were very slow. There were no in-line repeater amplifiers at the time, so telegraph speeds stayed at only 10 to 12 words per minute. The construction of the cables was also interesting. At the center was multi-stranded copper wire, covered with gutta-percha, then India rubber, and finally an outer layer of iron or steel wire. Gutta-percha is a natural polymer made from the sap of the Palaquium gutta tree. It was a nearly ideal insulator, stopping electric current from leaking into the water. It was so important that nothing replaced gutta-percha and rubber until polyethylene arrived in the 1930s.

Who dominated cables? The answer is Britain. From the 1850s until 1911, British systems dominated the most important market, the North Atlantic. The reason was clear: Britain had entrepreneurs ready to invest, and its wide colonial empire brought work from news agencies and trading companies. In 1892, two-thirds of the world's cables were run by British companies, and in 1896, 24 of the world's 30 cable-laying ships were British-owned. Geography also favored Britain, with Ireland on one side of the Atlantic and Newfoundland on the other, forming the shortest route across the ocean.

One note about the sources: one calls the cables that broke in 1929 telegraph cables, while another calls them telephone cables. The first transatlantic telephone cable system, TAT-1, began in 1956. In keeping with the Grand Banks material, we will call them telegraph cables. So where did the earth actually break?

articleEn: Now to the earthquake itself. It occurred in the Laurentian Slope seismic zone, which is why it is also called the Laurentian Slope earthquake. The center was at the edge of the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, about 400 kilometres south of the island, far from land in open ocean. The earthquake came with two faults, located about 250 kilometres south of the Burin Peninsula, and its moment magnitude was measured at 7.2.

The Burin Peninsula is about 130 kilometres long and juts out between Fortune Bay and Placentia Bay. It is also called The Boot. On land, the maximum intensity was VI on the Rossi-Forel scale, a strong tremor. But the real effect was on the seafloor.

The shaking was felt over a very wide area. People far from the epicenter felt it in New York City and Montreal. Tremors were also felt on Prince Edward Island, where intensity was reported between IV (slight tremor) and VI (strong tremor) on the Rossi-Forel scale. Another estimate put the province's intensity between III (weak) and V (moderate). Intensity was thus reported differently across places and scales.

In Saint Pierre and Miquelon, people were startled at about 16:30 by an earthquake that lasted around a minute. This French overseas territory lies about 18 kilometres west of the Burin Peninsula. There the intensity was V to VI on the Rossi-Forel scale.

The biggest effect was on the seabed. The earthquake set off a huge submarine landslide in which 200 cubic kilometres of material moved from its place, about 48 cubic miles. It is hard to grasp such a quantity, but this landslide becomes the center of the whole story. It was the largest submarine landslide recorded in Canada, up to 500 times bigger than the 1894 Saint-Alban subaerial slide. This landslide broke the 12 submarine cables. The greatest impacts on Newfoundland, Canada and Saint Pierre and Miquelon came from the cable breaks and the tsunami.

In 2002, Natural Resources Canada and the United States Geological Survey produced an intensity map of the earthquake using the Revised Modified Mercalli scale. On that scale, Saint Pierre and Miquelon experienced intensity IV (light) to V (moderate). The same earthquake's intensity was reported differently on different scales. So far we have seen how the ground shook. But the story of the sediment collapsing down the slope, tied to the silence of the cables, is still to come.

articleEn: A few minutes after the earthquake, a strange sequence began under the Atlantic. Cables broke one after another, each break farther away than the last. In all, 12 cables broke, and the breaks happened not in one place but at 28 locations in total. Some cables were cut in more than one place.

Most importantly, the exact time and place of each break was recorded. That record would later become the key to the puzzle. When the time of each cable break was noted, a map showed that the damage was moving from the epicenter down the slope. Investigators estimated that a flow of water-laden mud, a submarine landslide or turbidity current, moved downhill at about 100 km/h. It covered about 600 km of the continental slope, or 400 miles. Any cable in its path was broken.

Later research found that most of the slope failures occurred in water deeper than 650 meters, so the main action was at considerable depth. But the story was not limited to deep water. In shallower water, at just 5 to 25 meters, slumping also occurred, with sediment sliding downward. This shallow slumping turned into turbidity currents as it moved downslope. According to later research, these currents evolved ignitively, gaining strength as they advanced, and they lasted for several hours.

What was the cause? According to the sources, one reason was delayed retrogressive failure: part of the slope failed not immediately but after a delay. In addition, debris flows kept turning into turbidity currents through hydraulic jumps.

How did the mud flow travel so far? One answer lies in submarine canyons. When large turbidity currents enter canyons, they begin to sustain themselves and pick up sediment already deposited in the canyon. This is called canyon-flushing. The final volume of surges that begin from a slope failure can be many times larger than the failed section. Grand Banks is an example. To grasp the scale, 200 cubic kilometres of material moved in the landslide, the largest submarine landslide on record in Canada.

One interesting point: the sources disagree, with one calling these cables telegraph cables and another calling them telephone cables. The order in which the cables broke left, unintentionally, a trace of movement inside the ocean. But it would take time to read that trace. Was something also happening at the surface? Yes. In the next section we will see how the waves advanced toward the Burin Peninsula.

articleEn: Now let us turn to the surface. Below, sediment was sliding, and above, a tsunami had been born in the water and was heading toward the coast of Newfoundland. It arrived as three waves, with amplitudes between 3 and 8 meters, advancing quickly toward the shore. Runup means how high the water climbed on land. On the Burin Peninsula it was recorded at 13 meters. The distance from the epicenter to Burin was about 340 km, and the tsunami took 2 hours 23 minutes to cover it. These two figures give a sense of the speed.

Many settlements on the south coast were in its path. Many coastal communities on the peninsula were destroyed, and communication links were cut. According to the sources, many south coast communities were destroyed. 27 or 28 people died, and 1,000 or more were left homeless. The death toll is given as 27 or 28, and we will see that part of this difference comes from gaps in the record.

Now to Saint Pierre and Miquelon, French territory about 18 km west of the Burin Peninsula. People there were startled at about 16:30 by the earthquake, which lasted about a minute. About 50 minutes later the sea showed its next face. At 17:20 the tsunami reached the island of Saint-Pierre and the docks were flooded. The most damage was on the island then called Île-aux-Chiens, meaning Dog Island. After 1931 it was called L'Île-aux-Marins, the island of the sailors. The wave came from the south. It rose over the southern shore that protected the coast, and the low part of the island was flooded. Many houses and buildings were destroyed, and some moved from their places. Thankfully, no injuries or deaths were reported there.

The comparison between the two places is striking. On the Burin Peninsula there was loss of life, while in the islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon only buildings and docks were affected. The Burin Peninsula is about 130 km long and 15 to 30 km wide, a stretch of land reaching into the sea between Placentia Bay and Fortune Bay. Its economy has been tied to the sea for centuries. Cod and other fish were plentiful, so most settlements lay on the coast. The wave's runup reached 13 meters there and destroyed many south coast communities.
But after the destruction a new problem arose. How would help reach survivors when every link had been cut?

chapters.covers: Communication destroyed, blizzard next day, three days for S.S. Meigle to respond with supplies, doctors, nurses; donations about $250k; Dr. Mosdell's Loss of Life report, 27 deaths plus later additional one; no official victim list.

articleEn: After the tsunami, the greatest difficulty was silence. Electricity, radio and telegraph were unavailable for several days, and it was hard to get word out. Imagine it: settlements destroyed, a thousand or more people homeless, and every route to ask for help closed. Under the sea there was the silence of the cables, and on the coast there was the destruction of the settlements. Both stories were tied to the same earthquake.

The misfortune did not end there. The next day a blizzard struck the region, making relief efforts even harder. A distress signal was sent, but it took three days for a reply, when S.S. Meigle responded. It sent supplies, aid workers, a doctor, nurses, blankets and food. Help finally came by sea, the same sea that had brought the destruction. Yet three days of waiting was very long in those conditions.

Aid was not limited to one ship. Donations came from Newfoundland, the United States and the United Kingdom, totaling about $250k. In 2023 value, that is about CA$4.3 million, a considerable sum for its time.

How many people died in such a great disaster? Surprisingly, no complete list was ever made. According to the sources, no individual or body of the Newfoundland, French or British governments prepared an accurate or official list of victims. But one important document exists. Dr. Harris Munden Mosdell, chairman of the Burin West board of Health, wrote a report titled Loss of Life. In it he wrote that the total number of deaths from the tidal wave was 27. Of these, 25 deaths came directly from the upheaval. The other two came later, attributed to shock and exposure. So the report recorded a total of 27.

Later research linked one more death to the same earthquake. That may be why you find both 27 and 28. The report of the time recorded 27 deaths, and later research tied one more death to the earthquake. So the death toll is given as 27 or 28. In events like this, there are people behind the numbers. The families who lost their homes and loved ones deserve our attention and respect.
The waves did not stop at Newfoundland. They crossed the ocean, and in the next section we will look at their speeds.

articleEn: Now we arrive at 1952, about 23 years after the earthquake. Scientists at Columbia University did something interesting. They pieced together the fragments of the broken cables in order. Which cable broke when was the real clue. This work led to the discovery of the landslide, and for the first time a turbidity current was documented. The broken cables had revealed a hidden secret.

So what is a turbidity current? Simply put, it is sediment-laden water flowing down the ocean slope. It flows because the suspended sediment makes it denser than the surrounding water. The real force is gravity. On the way it scours the ground and picks up more sediment, like a snowball growing bigger, which can increase its speed further. When the current reaches the flat abyssal plain, sediment begins to settle. The layer deposited is called a turbidite.

Grand Banks is an example. In canyon-flushing, the final volume of the currents can be many times larger than the failed part of the slope. That is why cables at Grand Banks broke one after another. Investigators estimated that the flow moved at about 100 kilometres per hour. Later research says slope failures were mostly in water deeper than 650 meters. Slumping in shallower water went on to become turbidity currents. And these currents lasted for several hours, because the failure progressed backward in stages and debris flows kept turning into turbidity currents.

Remember that this understanding is still changing. According to 2018 research, water-laden sediment may be the real player in this process. Researchers at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute think the water flow is the final part of a process that begins at the seafloor.

Such currents have been seen in many places since Grand Banks. In the Cascadia subduction zone, 41 Holocene turbidity currents were linked along a plate boundary about 1000 kilometres long. The estimated interval between great earthquakes there is about 500 years in the north and about 240 years in the south. In Taiwan, during the 2006 Pingtung earthquake, 11 submarine cables broke in sequence. The current's speed there varied with the slope. On the steepest slope it was 20 meters per second and on the gentlest 3.7 meters per second. In other words, the steeper the slope, the faster the current. And the longest recorded turbidity current came in January 2020 in the Congo Canyon. It flowed 1,100 kilometres in 2 days and damaged 2 cables.

Now back to Newfoundland. Scientists also look for past tsunamis in layers of sand, to understand the regional frequency of big earthquakes. At Taylor's Bay, a sand layer was found that is believed to belong to the 1929 tsunami. It lay 13 centimetres below the turf line.

According to the source, after Grand Banks became the famous case of cable breaks, earthquake-generated turbidites were examined in many places. These include the Cascadia subduction zone, the Northern San Andreas Fault, Chile, Japan and many lakes. In this way the seafloor became a record of past earthquakes. Then, during the 2003 Tokachi-oki earthquake, a cabled observatory directly observed a large turbidity current. According to the source, this is very rare.

In a survey from 1959 to 1996, fewer than 9 percent of breaks were caused by natural events, so most causes were something else. And how important is this system? According to the source, submarine cables carry 99 percent of transoceanic data traffic, including internet and financial transactions.

Some questions are still not fully resolved. No accurate or official victims list for 1929 was ever prepared. The death toll is given as 27 or 28. And efforts continue to understand the regional frequency of big earthquakes from sand layers. The source also says the frequency of large tsunamis varies with the accumulation of offshore sediments, because in 1929 the power of the landslide gave birth to the wave.

shorts.text: سمندر کے نیچے 12 cables ایک کے بعد ایک ٹوٹتی گئیں۔ یہ 18 November 1929 کا دن تھا۔ Newfoundland کے جنوب میں آنے والے زلزلے کے چند منٹ بعد transatlantic cables ٹوٹنے لگیں۔ ہر break پچھلی سے زیادہ دور تھی۔ کل 12 cables، 28 جگہوں پر ٹوٹیں۔ ہر break کا صحیح وقت اور مقام record کیا گیا۔ نقشے پر دیکھا گیا کہ نقصان epicenter سے ڈھلوان کے نیچے کی طرف بڑھ رہا ہے۔ Investigators نے اندازہ لگایا کہ پانی سے بھری مٹی کا ایک بہاؤ تقریباً 100 km/h کی رفتار سے 600 km تک نیچے گیا۔ مگر یہ بہاؤ آخر تھا کیا؟ اس راز کا جواب کئی سال بعد ملا۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Samandar ke neeche 12 cables ek ke baad ek tootti gayin. Yeh 18 November 1929 ka din tha. Newfoundland ke junoob mein aane wale zalzale ke chand minute baad transatlantic cables tootne lagin. Har break pichli se zyada door thi. Kul 12 cables, 28 jagahon par tootin. Har break ka sahi waqt aur maqam record kiya gaya. Naqshe par dekha gaya ke nuqsan epicenter se dhalwan ke neeche ki taraf barh raha hai. Investigators ne andaza lagaya ke pani se bhari mitti ka ek bahao taqriban 100 km/h ki raftar se 600 km tak neeche gaya. Magar yeh bahao aakhir tha kya? Is raaz ka jawab kai saal baad mila. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

After the 1929 Grand Banks earthquake, 12 transatlantic cables broke in 28 places, one after another.
